name: Eastern Cape
summary_text: The Eastern Cape is listed among the former-Bantustan provinces where traditional-court jurisdiction operates—HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies the rural gender/sexual-rights exposure under customary adjudication—but no trans-specific incident, statute, enforcement action, or institutional statement was found for this province. The dossier states plainly: "Free State and Eastern Cape have no trans-specific source at all." Provincial violence against women and girls is severe (multiple 2025 mass-casualty killings in Gqeberha), but arrests followed each incident (four suspects for the May 2025 killings, four for the June 2025 burning of teenagers at KwaNobuhle, charges against a police officer for the July 2025 killings at Gordon Terrace), and none of the victims is identified as trans. The arrests represent a functioning—if strained—state-response mechanism, which is a small positive against the backdrop of extreme national violent-crime rates. For a visitor, the practical exposure is the general South African violent-crime baseline (national, priced into the 0.69) plus the township-and-rural customary-authority axis where a visibly gender-nonconforming person outside the metro NGO belt is more likely to encounter a chief's moral adjudication than a magistrate's court. No province-level ban, no enforcement against expression, no religious criminal law. The Constitutional Court's Mogale invalidity of the TKLA and the suspended replacement reduce but do not eliminate the parallel-system concern. The score is 0.02 below the national 0.69. vs. Limpopo (0.65) and North West (0.65), the Eastern Cape sits higher because its traditional-authority density is lower (the dossier groups Limpopo/North West as the provinces where "traditional-court jurisdiction actually bites" most strongly), and the 2025 arrests demonstrate at least nominally functioning state enforcement in the metro (Gqeberha). vs. Gauteng (0.71) and Western Cape (0.72), the gap reflects the absence of a metro NGO/prosecutor belt and the rural customary-authority geography. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), the Eastern Cape's lower deviation from national reflects the absence of a retrieved trans-specific study or royal/CONTRALESA episode in this province.

sources.title: The traditional courts bill threatens LGBT South Africans | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (fetch failed); the underlying HRW news analysis of the traditional-courts Bill (later enacted as the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act 3 of 2019) is explicit that it 'establishes a separate legal system for people living in the former Bantustans' and 'threatens to undermine this security for millions of South Africans living in rural areas', 'particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights', because chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law with a consent presumption running against the individual.
